body.text: Desk chair used as makeshift stretcher amid Queensland's ambulance ramping crisis
In short:
A lone paramedic wheeled a woman who had waited 12 hours for an ambulance to a 4WD on an office chair.
Another woman was driven to the emergency room by an urgent care doctor during a "medical emergency" after an ambulance did not arrive.
A Far North Queensland-based paramedic said he was "genuinely worried about the consequences" of hospital ramping.

After Liz Cullen fell heavily at her central Queensland home, she pushed through excruciating pain to shuffle along the floor and pull herself up on one leg to reach her mobile phone and dial Triple Zero (000).

In tears because of the "10-out-of-10" pain in her right knee, the 63-year-old, who lives alone, expected she may have to wait a couple of hours for an ambulance after she was told paramedics would get to her "as soon as possible".
But it took all day for the Queensland Ambulance Service (QAS) to arrive – a sole paramedic in a 4WD without a stretcher.

Ms Cullen is one of many people affected by Queensland's ongoing ambulance ramping crisis—when paramedics wait with patients for more than 30 minutes before hospital emergency department staff can take over care.
The issue affects not only patients on the ramp—it also prevents paramedics from reaching others in the community.
Twelve-hour wait
An independent review has been promised into the death this month of 51-year-old Nick Bradford in Brisbane.
Mr Bradford, who also lived alone, phoned for an ambulance complaining of chest pains. By the time paramedics arrived more than two hours later, he was dead.
Twelve hours after Ms Cullen's initial Triple Zero call on September 12, a senior paramedic driving a 4WD pulled up outside her Rockhampton home.
The QAS insists the 4WD is "an ambulance", because it was driven by a paramedic, is fitted with lights and sirens and carries equipment to respond to incidents.
It had no stretcher but by that stage, Ms Cullen was willing to "get to hospital any way I could" after the lone paramedic told her an ambulance was still hours away.
"He was very apologetic," Ms Cullen said.
Unable to walk, Ms Cullen was wheeled to the 4WD in an office chair and driven to Rockhampton Hospital.
By that stage, Ms Cullen's daughter was with her.
In the hours before the paramedics arrived, her daughter helped her to the toilet and brought her a glass of water.
But getting her mother out of the house was too much.
"I was in so much pain, and I have a little lip to get over at the front door," Ms Cullen said.
When she finally got to hospital, the senior paramedic had to double-park and find a wheelchair to take Ms Cullen inside.
There, she said she was met with stretchers and paramedics lining both sides of the emergency department and down a hallway.
"Out in the actual waiting room, it was choc-a-block full as well," Ms Cullen said.
"There were people getting quite angry out there that had obviously been waiting a while, too. I think it's just too busy in that emergency department."
Ms Cullen ended up staying three nights in hospital with a torn meniscus — damage to cartilage that protects the knee joint — which required surgery.
"I was assessed by a physiotherapist who said that they couldn't send me home because I lived alone and I couldn't weight bear," she said.
She was operated on privately earlier this month.
Patients fending for themselves
About 1,000km north, in Cairns, former nurse Jill Knell, 71, took herself to her local Medicare Urgent Care Clinic at 9pm on October 15 after feeling unwell most of the day.
There, her blood pressure was tested several times at 220/100 — a reading she describes as "a medical emergency".
"It can be life-threatening because it could be indicative of a stroke, a heart attack, an aneurysm, or acute kidney failure," Ms Knell said.
The doctor gave her some blood pressure lowering tablets and phoned an ambulance about 9:50pm, 10 minutes before the clinic closed.
"There was a nurse and a receptionist and doctor. None of them could go home because they couldn't leave me," Ms Knell said.
She told them she could wait in her car for the ambulance to come but the staff said they would wait with her.
More than two hours later, it still had not arrived.
At midnight, when the QAS could not tell the doctor when an ambulance would be sent, he put Ms Knell, who also lives alone, in his own car and drove her to Cairns Hospital himself.
They arrived about 20 minutes past midnight.
The Urgent Care doctor handed her over to emergency department staff and requested that she be able to lie down, but there were no beds.
"I was told there could be a significant wait as there was severe ambulance ramping but that I should not leave," Ms Knell said.
Outside of Brisbane, Cairns Hospital is one of the state's worst hospitals for ambulance ramping.

In August, the latest data available, 45.6 per cent of patients arriving by ambulance were ramped — worse than the August before the Crisafulli government came to power in 2024, when it was 37 per cent.

Ms Knell had her blood pressure checked about 20 minutes after she arrived at the emergency department, a nurse drew blood, and she had an electrocardiogram (ECG) to test the electrical activity of her heart. She was also given a strong painkiller.
"I was then left alone in a chair in the chaotic waiting room unmonitored for nearly two hours," she said.
"I was feeling seriously unwell, had a terrible headache, was nauseous, exhausted and had palpitations."
At her request, a nurse checked her blood pressure again at 2:50am.
Ms Knell was feeling "even more nauseous, woozy and desperate to lie down" but her blood pressure had gone down.

At 3:20am, about three hours after arriving at the hospital, she had another blood pressure check with a similarly lower reading, then discharged herself without seeing a doctor "due to the distressing waiting room environment and the anticipated long wait ahead".
She consulted her own general practitioner (GP) later that day, who ordered a brain scan to check for signs of a stroke, and has been under the GP's care since.
Blame directed at system
A Far North Queensland-based paramedic, who wanted to remain anonymous, said he was "genuinely worried about the consequences" of hospital ramping on the region.
"I fear it is only a matter of time before a patient falls through the gaps in the system and suffers a serious adverse outcome, potentially resulting in death," he said.
"It is deeply troubling to feel that it may take a preventable tragedy before meaningful action is taken."
Neither Ms Knell nor Ms Cullen is angry with the individuals who cared for them.
"The ambulance and medical staff as individuals were absolutely doing their best in an obviously failing, unsustainable and unacceptable environment," Ms Knell said.
Both women have written letters of complaint to their regional public hospitals.
"It's the hospital system that I blame," Ms Cullen said.
A QAS spokesman said the service was "committed to delivering the best care possible and will always prioritise the sickest patients first".
He said staff assessed both patients based on the information provided and "received appropriate clinical oversight" during very busy periods.
